title: Case study: Analyzing a stock, step by step
subtitle: Stock analysis example
openingQuestion: Analyzing FPT, you see its current P/E is 22x, while the technology sector average is 18x. What does that mean?
openingOptions: A P/E above the sector average always, with no exception, means the stock will fall sharply in the near future
FPT is definitely a poor-quality business and investors should avoid it entirely based on a single above-sector P/E
The market is pricing FPT above the sector, and growth needs a closer look
The P/E ratio carries no practical analytical meaning at all when applied to technology-sector stocks
explanation: A P/E above the sector average isn't automatically a bad or good signal - it can reflect higher expected growth (reasonable) or overpricing (risky). P/E needs to be read alongside profit growth, earnings quality, and other metrics for a fuller picture.

realWorldExample.description: FPT is Vietnam's leading technology group, operating across three main segments: technology (software outsourcing, digital transformation), telecom (fiber internet, pay TV), and education. It's one of the large-cap, highly liquid stocks new investors often pick to practice fundamental analysis, thanks to a transparent financial history, steady multi-year growth, and easily accessible financial statements.

quiz.question: When analyzing a company's revenue and profit over several years, what matters most to watch for?
options: There's no need to compare against other companies in the same sector
Revenue always matters more than profit in every case, a distinction worth checking before relying on it
Only the most recent year's figures matter; earlier years can be ignored
The multi-year growth trend matters more than any single year
quiz.explanation: One good profit year can come from a one-off event (asset sale, provision reversal...) that won't repeat. A stable growth trend over 3-5 consecutive years reflects the real health of the business far better than a single year.

quiz.question: How is the P/E (Price-to-Earnings) ratio calculated, and what does it basically mean?
options: P/E = Share price / EPS; the price paid for each dong of profit
P/E = Revenue / the company's current market capitalization, though the reasoning behind it is easy to miss
P/E = Total assets / Total debt, a measure of financial safety
P/E is fixed at the same value for every stock on the same exchange
quiz.explanation: P/E equals the market price per share divided by earnings per share (EPS). It's one of the most common valuation ratios, used to compare how 'expensive or cheap' stocks are relative to peers in the same sector.

quiz.question: Why is the dividend payout ratio also useful information when analyzing a stock?
options: Because dividends always matter more than the profit growth rate, even without checking whether the company's payout ratio is unusually low or high
Because it shows whether the company distributes profit or reinvests it
Because the payout ratio has no connection to financial health at all, a detail many overlook at first glance
Because a payout ratio above 50% is required for a company to be good
quiz.explanation: A high dividend payout ratio is common among mature businesses with fewer new growth opportunities, so they prioritize returning cash to shareholders. A low or zero payout ratio is common among fast-growing businesses that prioritize retaining profit to reinvest in expansion.

quiz.question: A company's revenue grows 25% a year, but operating cash flow is negative and receivables are up 60%. What's the most sensible reading?
options: Negative cash flow is normal for any business in an expansion phase, which is not obvious without reading closely
Strong revenue growth always offsets negative cash flow in the short run
The growth may be coming from looser credit terms extended to customers
Fast-rising receivables show the company is collecting cash more efficiently than before
quiz.explanation: Receivables growing faster than revenue means each new dong of revenue is arriving more slowly - a classic sign of buying growth with easy credit terms. It isn't always bad, but it's a question that has to be answered before trusting the 25% figure.

quiz.question: Why does comparing a real-estate company's P/E with a software company's P/E lead to almost no conclusion?
options: Because the software sector's profit is always higher, so its P/E is always lower
Because real-estate companies aren't allowed to disclose earnings per share
Because P/E can only be applied to companies listed on the same exchange, and only compares two firms that happen to share the exact same growth rate
Because the two sectors differ sharply in growth rate, risk level, and capital intensity
quiz.explanation: P/E is the market price paid for each dong of profit, and that price depends on expected growth, stability, and the capital required to grow. When two sectors differ on all three, a P/E gap is expected, not a sign of over- or under-pricing.

keyTakeaways: Fundamental stock analysis should run through at least four steps: multi-year revenue/profit trend, valuation (P/E vs. sector), dividends, and sector outlook
A stable growth trend across several years matters more than one attractive single-year figure
A P/E above the sector average isn't automatically bad - it needs to be read alongside the expected profit growth rate
There's no single correct formula for every stock; fundamental analysis combines several angles into a more grounded decision than guessing

practicePrompt.question: You're analyzing company Z: revenue has grown steadily at 15%/year for the past 5 years, current P/E is 20x (sector average 16x), and the dividend payout ratio is low because it's building a new factory. Which assessment is most sensible?
options: All four factors need to be weighed together before concluding, since a high P/E can reflect growth expectations
This stock is certainly overpriced and should be avoided entirely just because its P/E is 4 points above the sector average
The low dividend payout ratio is the only bad sign worth caring about; the other factors don't need further review
Steady 15%/year revenue growth alone is enough to conclude this is a good investment opportunity
practicePrompt.explanation: Fundamental stock analysis needs to combine several factors - a P/E above the sector can be reasonable when paired with steady revenue growth and a low payout ratio driven by reinvestment for expansion.

application.title: Analyze a real stock
application.message: Pick a listed company you're interested in, and walk through the four steps yourself: the revenue/profit trend of the last few years, P/E versus the sector, dividend policy, and sector outlook.
application.secondary: Doing this once, following the process, will make you much faster and more confident the next time.

sections.text: Having learned the theory of P/E, ROE, dividends, and other concepts in earlier lessons, it's time to assemble them into a real analysis process. Let's walk through each step with a concrete example: the FPT stock.
Step 1: Understand what the business does

Before looking at any number, you need to understand how the business makes money. FPT has three main segments: technology (the largest share of revenue and profit, mainly from software exports to Japan, the US, and Europe, plus digital transformation services), telecom (fiber internet, pay TV - a stable segment with steady cash flow), and education (FPT's university and school system - a fast-growing segment thanks to rising demand for education).
Step 2: Look at the multi-year revenue and profit trend

Instead of only looking at the most recent quarterly report, look at the trend over 3-5 consecutive years. A business whose revenue and after-tax profit have grown steadily at 15-20%/year across several consecutive years (as FPT has shown in the 2019-2024 period) points to a stable business model that doesn't depend on one-off events.
Step 3: Value it with P/E - comparison needs context

P/E = Share price / Earnings per share (EPS). If FPT trades at a P/E of 22x while the technology sector averages around 18x, don't rush to conclude FPT is 'expensive' or 'cheap'. Ask instead: does FPT's profit growth rate exceed the sector average? If FPT's profit grows 20%/year while the sector grows only 10%/year, the higher P/E may still be reasonable - this is the logic behind the PEG ratio (P/E divided by the growth rate).
Step 4: Look at dividends and profit-distribution policy

FPT has a history of paying dividends regularly every year, combining cash and stock bonuses, reflecting a business that already has stable cash flow but still retains part of its profit to reinvest in growth segments (such as data centers and AI). A moderate dividend payout ratio (neither too high nor zero) is often a sign of a business balancing shareholder rewards with sustaining growth.

items: Step 1: Understand the business model - where the company makes its money, which segment carries the largest share
Step 2: Look at the revenue and profit trend over 3-5 consecutive years, not just one year
Step 3: Value it with P/E, compare against the sector average, and set it against the growth rate
Step 4: Look at dividend policy - it reflects the business's development stage and strategic priorities
Step 5 (extra): Assess sector risk and competitive position - what edge does FPT have over rivals, and does the technology sector carry any cyclical risk

sections.label: Important note: this is an illustration of a process, not investment advice
sections.text: This case study illustrates HOW to think through fundamental analysis via concrete steps, not a recommendation to buy or sell FPT stock. Financial figures change over time, and every investor needs to update the latest financial statements and check them against their own goals and risk appetite before making a real decision.

lines: Fundamental stock analysis isn't about finding one 'magic' number - it's about assembling several pieces of information (profit trend, valuation, dividends, sector position) into a grounded picture.
Apply this 4-5 step process properly to any stock you're interested in, rather than buying on impulse or rumor.
